panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph demonstrating established Volkmann ischemic contracture with visible wrist flexion deformity and digital stiffness (claw hand), along with elbow flexion contracture and fixed forearm pronation. B: Clinical photograph showing Volkmann ischemic contracture with characteristic proximal forearm ischemic scarring, forearm muscle atrophy, wrist stiffness, and finger flexion deformity.

panels.figure_caption: Preoperative clinical appearance of the left upper limb. (A) Lateral view showing severe elbow flexion contracture, fixed forearm pronation, wrist deformity, and digital stiffness secondary to established Volkmann ischemic contracture. The arrow highlights the elbow flexion contracture and wrist-hand deformity. (B) Anterolateral view demonstrating proximal forearm scarring, forearm amyotrophy, wrist stiffness, and flexion deformity of the fingers before staged reconstructive surgery. The arrow highlights the proximal forearm scar.
in_text_mentions: Neurological examination revealed paresthesia involving the thumb and index finger. Motor examination showed severe stiffness of the elbow, wrist, and fingers, with loss of active wrist extension, absent useful active flexion of the proximal interphalangeal joints of the four ulnar fingers, and absent thumb opposition, flexion, and extension. The preoperative clinical appearance is shown in Figure 1.

Visual: the fingers are flexed in a contracted, claw-like posture.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Panel is a real preoperative clinical photograph from a child with article-level Volkmann ischemic contracture; the visible fixed wrist and finger flexion contracture support the diagnosis. b: Nerve ultrasound of the same child with Volkmann ischemic contracture shows an arrow-marked ulnar nerve abnormality; the text confirms ulnar nerve affection after suspected compartment syndrome. c: Forearm-level ulnar nerve ultrasound in the same child with Volkmann ischemic contracture shows the described nerve affection approximately 7 cm distal to the ulnar epicondyle.

in_text_mentions: Diagnostics included a magnetic resonance (MR) angiography, an X-ray of the forearm, repeated nerve conduction velocity assessments, and sonography of the nerves ( Fig. 1b, c ) and muscles of the forearm. They revealed an injury to the median nerve at the elbow joint and muscle deterioration in both flexor muscle compartments with the ulnar nerve's affection 7 cm distally to the ulnar epicondyle following the suspected compartment syndrome. plate_findings.evidence: The long finger shows severe flexion contracture, and the ring finger shows a mild flexion contracture with the wrist in the neutral position

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Preoperative clinical photo of left hand in neutral wrist position showing severe long finger and mild ring finger flexion contracture in case report titled Localized type Volkmann's contracture; classic Volkmann tenodesis effect. B: Same hand different view with wrist neutral showing fixed flexion contracture of long and ring fingers consistent with localized Volkmann ischemic contracture. C: Same hand with wrist in palmar flexion demonstrating reduction of finger flexion contractures - Volkmann tenodesis sign supporting localized Volkmann ischemic contracture.
panels.attribution_text: Kaji et al. Localized type Volkmann's contracture treated with tendon transfer and tension-reduced early mobilization: A case report.. Medicine 2017. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000005807. CC BY-ND (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nd/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative findings of the left hand. (A, B) The long finger shows severe flexion contracture, and the ring finger shows a mild flexion contracture with the wrist in the neutral position. (C) The flexion contractures of these 2 fingers are reduced with the wrist in the palmar flexion position.
in_text_mentions: ysical examination, the long finger of the left hand demonstrated severe flexion contractures, and the ring finger demonstrated a mild flexion contracture with the wrist in the neutral position (Fig. 1 A and B). However, the flexion contractures of these 2 fingers were reduced with the wrist in the palmar flexion position (Fig. 1C). The ranges of motion of the thumb, index, and little finger were normal.
